Original Plan: Directly study whether spread volatility increases
New Evidence / Problem: Individual stock volatility is already rising; directly studying spread volatility increase is almost trivially true
Reason for Adjustment: Controlled for individual stock volatility; changed to study "excess spread volatility relative to individual stock volatility"
What I Learned: Research design must control for confounding variables; otherwise conclusions have no information value

Original Plan: Use 44 pairs to run separate regressions on three test periods
New Evidence / Problem: Only 44 data points per period, regression not significant
What Was Tested: Tried pooled regression (176 data points); also used 28 updated pairs as robustness check to rule out pair aging
Reason for Adjustment: Pooled regression is significant but smooths period differences, only used as supplement; updated pairs used to verify whether conclusions are driven by pair aging
What I Learned: There is a trade-off between sample size and statistical power; pair relationships change over time and require rolling updates

Original Plan: Assumed excess spread volatility in test2 was a widespread phenomenon
New Evidence / Problem: Test2 residual median was negative (-0.0704), kurtosis extremely high (38.79)
What Was Tested: Checked residual distribution and concentration; found AAPL-HPE contributed 79.3% of positive residuals
Reason for Adjustment: Excess expansion is driven by a few extreme pairs; need to separate extreme and normal pairs for layered analysis
What I Learned: Group definitions based on results are necessary but require attention to selection bias

Original Plan: Assumed p-value increase means pair relationship breakdown; four indicators told inconsistent stories
New Evidence / Problem: p-value already rose broadly in test1 (median > 0.38); Hurst decreased, half-life stable/extended, correlation rose
What Was Tested: Calculated cointegration p-values across periods; examined the meaning of each indicator
Reason for Adjustment: p-value increase does not equal relationship breakdown, may be a statistical artifact from beta drift; beta drift explains the contradictions: it causes p-value increase and half-life extension, but Hurst still shows mean reversion
What I Learned: Cannot judge pair relationships from a single indicator; different indicators measure different dimensions and need to be interpreted together

Original Plan: Assumed all pairs were breaking down
New Evidence / Problem: Normal and extreme pairs had different recovery rates
What Was Tested: Recalculated p-values using test-period beta; compared recovery rates between the two groups
Reason for Adjustment: In test3, 48% of normal pairs recovered, but only 20% of extreme pairs recovered, showing normal pairs' p-value increase is mainly driven by beta drift, while extreme pairs may genuinely break down
What I Learned: Normal and extreme pairs are fundamentally different

Original Plan: Originally planned to use fixed beta for profitability
New Evidence / Problem: Found beta drifts persistently; fixed beta fails; literature shows beta drift is widespread and Kalman filter is a must
Reason for Adjustment: Switched to Kalman filter to dynamically track beta; delta=1e-3 performed best in test1 and test2, 5e-3 close behind
What I Learned: Method selection should be based on data characteristics
